7624: Before anything else, picture a plane soaring high above the clouds — far above everything else on the ground. That image of being elevated above the rest is the heart of this word. Everything "high-flying" means flows from that single image.

In its simplest, most direct sense, "high-flying" describes something that actually flies at a great height.

"A high-flying jet streaked across the sky."
"The eagle is a high-flying bird."

This literal use is rare in modern English. You won't see it very often. It mostly lives in the background as the origin of the word's more common meaning.
Meaning 2 — The Figurative Meaning (the main one)

This is the meaning you will encounter almost every time you see "high-flying" in real life. Here, the word has nothing to do with actual flight. Instead, it describes a person, career, or lifestyle that has reached — or is actively climbing toward — a very high level of success, status, or achievement.

Just like a plane flying high is above all others, a "high-flying" person is above most others in terms of accomplishment and ambition.

When used to describe a person, it means someone who is exceptionally driven, ambitious, and successful — typically in their professional life.

"She is a high-flying lawyer at one of the most prestigious firms in the country."
"He was a high-flying executive who managed thousands of employees."

Both sentences paint a picture of someone who has climbed very high in their field.

When used to describe a career or lifestyle, it suggests a life or career that is fast-paced, glamorous, competitive, and associated with great achievement.

"After years of living a high-flying lifestyle, she longed for a quiet, simple life."
"He left his high-flying career in finance to become a teacher."

Notice how these sentences carry a sense of prestige — but also, subtly, a sense of pressure and exhaustion. That undertone is real and intentional.

"High-flying" has one more dimension worth knowing. When attached to ambitions, promises, claims, or ideas, it can suggest that something is impressively grand on the surface — but possibly too idealistic, unrealistic, or disconnected from reality.

Think of it this way: a plane flying extremely high is impressive to look at, but it is also very far from the ground — far from reality, far from solid earth.

"The politician made high-flying promises that he had no real plan to keep."
"The company had high-flying ambitions but lacked the funding to back them up."

In these sentences, "high-flying" carries a gentle, skeptical tone — a quiet warning that something sounds great, but may not hold up in the real world.

This shade of meaning is context-dependent. It only appears when the word is attached to ideas, rhetoric, or promises — not when it describes a person's career or success.

In most cases, "high-flying" is admiring and positive. Calling someone a high-flying professional is a compliment — it means they are impressive, driven, and successful.

But it can also carry a very slight hint of criticism or envy. Saying someone has a "high-flying lifestyle" can sometimes subtly suggest they are out of touch with ordinary people, or that their success has come with a cost.

The word is almost never harshly negative — but it is not always purely neutral either. Context is everything.
Who and What This Word Describes

"High-flying" is almost always placed directly before a noun. Here are the most natural and common combinations you'll encounter in real English:

People: a high-flying executive, lawyer, banker, entrepreneur, professional, graduate

Careers and lifestyles: a high-flying career, a high-flying lifestyle, a high-flying world

Ideas and claims: high-flying ambitions, high-flying rhetoric, high-flying promises, high-flying goals
The One Rule to Always Remember

Whenever you see "high-flying," ask yourself one question: What has been elevated here?

If it's a person or career → they have risen very high in success and status.
If it's ideas or promises → they sound grand and impressive, but may be dangerously far from the ground — from reality.

That single question will always unlock the correct meaning, no matter the context.
7625:
High-handed describes a way of behaving where someone uses their power, authority, or position in an arrogant, bossy, and dismissive way — without caring about what others think, feel, or deserve. The person acts as though their judgment is the only one that matters, and as though the rights, opinions, or feelings of others can simply be pushed aside.

It always carries a negative meaning. You would never use "high-handed" as a compliment. It is always a criticism.

Picture someone who has a certain amount of power — a boss, a government official, a landlord, a manager, a parent — and instead of using that power carefully and fairly, they just do whatever they want, however they want, without consulting anyone or following proper process. They bulldoze through decisions. They dismiss objections. They act as though everyone else should simply fall in line and be quiet. That is the essence of being high-handed.

The key is not just that they're tough or strict. It's that they're arrogant about it. They don't just act alone — they act as though it's their absolute right to act alone, and as though anyone who questions them is out of place.
What makes something "high-handed" — the three ingredients

Three elements are almost always present:

First, there is some power or authority — real or assumed. A completely powerless person can't really be high-handed; the word implies someone who has some lever of control over others.

Second, there is disregard — a deliberate or careless ignoring of others' rights, feelings, input, or proper procedure. The high-handed person doesn't just happen to overlook others; they don't consider others to be worth consulting in the first place.

Third, there is arrogance — a sense that their way is the only way, and that resistance or objection is simply not acceptable.

Remove any one of these, and you're describing something else. It's the combination of power + disregard + arrogance that makes something high-handed.

A company CEO sends an email on a Friday evening announcing that 300 employees are laid off, effective immediately, with no prior warning, no discussion, no due process. Critics call this high-handed — brutal, dismissive, and showing total disregard for the dignity of the workers.

A local government decides to demolish a historic building to build a parking lot, and does so without a single public meeting or community consultation, ignoring the protests of residents. This is a high-handed decision.

A landlord discovers a tenant has a small pet, which wasn't in the lease. Instead of discussing it, he simply shows up, changes the lock, and leaves a note saying "You violated the rules. You have 24 hours to collect your things." That is high-handed behavior.

A senior doctor dismisses a junior nurse's concerns about a patient's medication without even listening to her reasoning, saying, "I've been doing this for 30 years. Just follow the prescription." High-handed.

In each case, notice that the person isn't simply being decisive or even harsh — they are actively treating the other party as though their input, rights, or dignity doesn't deserve consideration.
High-handed vs. words it might be confused with

It helps to distinguish "high-handed" from similar words.

Strict means having high standards and enforcing rules firmly — but a strict person can still be fair, listen to others, and follow proper procedure. A high-handed person doesn't bother with any of that.

Decisive means making choices quickly and confidently — a positive quality. A high-handed person might look decisive, but the difference is that decisiveness respects due process and others' roles, while high-handedness bulldozes over them.

Bossy is informal and slightly milder — a bossy person likes to give orders. A high-handed person goes further: they act as though they have the absolute right to impose their will, and any resistance is illegitimate.

Autocratic and dictatorial are close in meaning and are the strongest synonyms — they emphasize total, unilateral control. High-handed is slightly softer, and is more often used to describe specific decisions or behaviors rather than an entire style of governance.
How it is used in sentences

High-handed is typically used to describe either a person or their actions/decisions.

Describing a person: "The new principal was high-handed and refused to involve teachers in any decisions." Here it describes a general characteristic of the person.

Describing an action or decision: "The court ruled that the eviction had been high-handed and unlawful." Here it describes a specific thing that was done.

You will also frequently see it in the phrase "high-handed manner" or "high-handed approach" — as in, "He dealt with the complaint in a very high-handed manner."
The other forms of the word

High-handedly is the adverb: "She high-handedly overruled every suggestion the team made."

High-handedness is the noun: "The high-handedness of the authorities drew widespread public outrage."

If you ever want to quickly check whether "high-handed" fits, ask: Is this person using their power arrogantly, without caring about fairness, proper process, or the rights and feelings of others? If yes — that's high-handed.
7626:
When you call someone high-minded, you are saying that they have strong moral principles and noble ideals — that they genuinely care about doing what is right, good, and ethical, often even when it is difficult or costly for them personally.

Think of it this way: just as "high" suggests being above the ordinary level, a high-minded person's values and thinking are above petty, selfish, or dishonest behaviour. They aim for what is morally excellent, not just what is convenient.
The Two Faces of This Word

This is the most important thing to understand: "high-minded" can be used in two ways — one genuinely positive, and one subtly critical. The meaning shifts depending on the context and the tone of the speaker.

① The Positive Sense (Admiring)

Here, it means someone who is genuinely principled, idealistic, and morally serious — in a way that you respect and admire.

"She was a high-minded leader who refused to accept bribes even when everyone around her did."

"His high-minded commitment to justice inspired the whole community."

In this sense, the word praises the person. They have real values, they stick to them, and their ideals are authentic.

② The Slightly Critical Sense (Mocking or Doubting)

Here, "high-minded" carries a gentle sarcasm. It suggests someone whose ideals are too lofty, impractical, or self-righteous — someone who talks about noble principles but is out of touch with reality, or who moralises at others while not necessarily being perfect themselves.

"His high-minded speech about poverty was met with eye-rolls — he had never struggled a day in his life."

"She dismissed it with high-minded talk about ethics, but offered no real solutions."

In this sense, the word quietly mocks the person. The ideals sound grand but feel hollow, disconnected from real life, or even a little arrogant.

How do you know which sense is being used? Read the surrounding tone. If the writer or speaker sounds respectful and sincere, it's sense ①. If they sound ironic, frustrated, or dismissive, it's sense ②.
What Does a High-Minded Person Actually Look Like?

Here are real-world examples to make this feel concrete:

  • A politician who refuses to run a dirty campaign even when it could cost them the election — because they believe in honest politics.
  • A business owner who pays their workers fairly even when cutting wages would make them richer — because they believe people deserve dignity.
  • A student who refuses to cheat on an exam even when everyone else is doing it — because they hold themselves to a higher standard.
  • A person who is always lecturing others about recycling, diet, or social justice but never listens or compromises — this would be the more critical, negative sense.

The word has a somewhat formal and serious tone. You won't usually hear it in casual conversation like "Oh, he's so high-minded." It appears more often in writing, speeches, journalism, and literature. When used, it immediately signals that something morally significant is being discussed.

Knowing related words helps you understand a word more deeply:

  • Principled — guided by clear moral rules
  • Idealistic — believing strongly in noble ideals (often with a hint of impracticality)
  • Noble — having fine personal qualities and high moral character
  • Righteous — morally right and virtuous
  • Magnanimous — generous and forgiving in spirit
  • Self-righteous (negative) — smugly certain that one is morally superior (this captures the negative side of high-minded perfectly)
  • Preachy (negative) — too eager to lecture others about morality

• Unprincipled — having no moral standards
  • Self-serving — motivated purely by personal gain
  • Cynical — believing people are always motivated by selfish interests
  • Petty — concerned with small, trivial, or mean things
  • Corrupt — willing to act dishonestly for personal benefit

High-minded = having high moral ideals and principles — admirable when genuine, slightly ridiculous when it becomes arrogant or out of touch with reality.

Once you hold both sides of this word in your head, you'll always understand it perfectly — no matter where or how you encounter it.
7627:
Think of the word "power" — it means strength, force, or the ability to do a lot. Now add "high" to it. High-powered simply means having a very large amount of power — whether that power is physical (like in a machine) or personal (like in a person's career or influence).

The word is used in two main ways: one literal (about machines and equipment) and one figurative (about people, jobs, and events).

When "high-powered" describes a machine, tool, or piece of equipment, it means that the thing produces a very large amount of energy, force, or capability — far more than an ordinary version of the same thing.

Examples:

  • A high-powered rifle — a gun that shoots with extreme force and can hit targets far away.
  • A high-powered engine — an engine that is much stronger and faster than a regular one.
  • A high-powered microscope — a microscope that can zoom in so closely that you can see things invisible to the naked eye.
  • A high-powered laser — a laser beam so strong it can cut through metal.

The key idea here is intensity of output. A high-powered machine doesn't just work — it works with far greater force or capability than average.

This is the most common way the word is used in everyday English. When "high-powered" describes a person, it means someone who is:

  • Very successful in their professional field
  • Influential — their decisions affect many people
  • Driven and ambitious — they work extremely hard and aim for the top
  • Important — they often hold senior, prestigious positions

Examples:

  • A high-powered lawyer — not just any lawyer, but one who handles major cases, earns a lot of money, and is highly respected or feared in their field.
  • A high-powered executive — a senior business leader who makes big decisions that shape a company.
  • A high-powered politician — someone with real authority and influence over policy and government.

Think of it this way: if you lined up ten lawyers in a room, the high-powered one is the one the others look up to — the one with the most wins, the biggest clients, and the most authority.

Important nuance: "High-powered" for a person is not just about being good at their job. It also carries a sense of intensity and drive. A high-powered person is typically someone who works relentlessly, is very competitive, and operates in demanding, high-stakes environments.
Meaning 3 — Figurative: Jobs, Careers, and Lifestyles

When "high-powered" describes a job, career, or way of life, it means something that is:

  • Demanding and intense — it requires enormous effort, focus, and time
  • High-stakes — the decisions made have serious consequences
  • Prestigious and well-compensated — but often stressful

Examples:

  • A high-powered career in finance — a career that is lucrative and respected, but involves long hours and constant pressure.
  • A high-powered lifestyle — a life full of important meetings, business travel, big decisions, and very little downtime.
  • A high-powered job — a role with a lot of responsibility, visibility, and pressure to perform.

Notice that with jobs and lifestyles, "high-powered" has a slight double edge — it sounds impressive, but it also implies that the person is under a lot of pressure or stress.

"High-powered" can also describe meetings, negotiations, discussions, or gatherings where the people involved are very important or influential.

Examples:

  • A high-powered meeting — a meeting attended by senior executives, world leaders, or other very important figures where major decisions are made.
  • A high-powered summit — a gathering of powerful world leaders to discuss critical global issues.
  • A high-powered negotiation — a deal discussion involving massive amounts of money or influence, with very high stakes on both sides.

The word signals that this is not an ordinary event — the participants are influential, the stakes are high, and the outcomes matter.
The Tone and Feeling of the Word

"High-powered" is generally a positive or impressive-sounding word, but it almost always carries an undertone of intensity and seriousness. It is rarely used lightly or casually.

  • It suggests the person or thing operates above the average level.
  • It implies prestige, but also pressure.
  • It is used to set someone or something apart as belonging to an elite, demanding category.

You will most often hear or read "high-powered" in front of these words:

People: lawyer, attorney, executive, businessperson, consultant, lobbyist, agent, broker, politician

Jobs/Lifestyles: career, job, lifestyle, position, role

Events: meeting, negotiation, summit, conference

Equipment: rifle, engine, microscope, computer, laser, telescope
A Simple Way to Remember It

If something is high-powered, it operates with more force, influence, or intensity than most things of its kind — whether it's a machine, a person, a job, or an event.

Whenever you see "high-powered," ask yourself: "Is this being described as unusually strong, influential, or demanding?" The answer will almost always be yes — and that's exactly what the word means.
7628:
When something or someone is described as high-profile, it means they attract a large amount of public attention. They are widely noticed, widely talked about, and widely covered — especially in the news and media. The word paints a picture of a bright spotlight shining on someone or something, making them very visible to the world.

Think of it this way: imagine a stadium with thousands of people. A person sitting quietly in the crowd is "low-profile" — almost nobody notices them. But the star player running on the field, with cameras flashing and crowds cheering? That person is high-profile.

The adjective "high-profile" can describe a person, an event, a case, a job, or a situation. The common thread is always the same: a lot of eyes are on it.

  • A high-profile person is someone who is very famous, powerful, or influential — a celebrity, a top politician, a CEO of a major company, or anyone the public talks about a lot.
  • A high-profile case (often used in law) is a legal trial or investigation that the public and media are following very closely — perhaps because the crime was shocking, or because the people involved are famous.
  • A high-profile event is one that gets enormous attention — a major international summit, a championship game, a royal wedding.
  • A high-profile job or role is a position where you are constantly in the public eye and your actions are closely watched — like being the president of a country, the head coach of a famous sports team, or the spokesperson for a major organization.

The heart of "high-profile" is visibility. It does not necessarily mean good or bad, successful or unsuccessful, important or unimportant. It simply means: many people are aware of it and paying attention to it. A high-profile scandal is just as "high-profile" as a high-profile achievement — both are being watched closely by a large audience.

However, in practice, the word does carry a subtle flavor of significance. Things that are high-profile tend to feel weighty and consequential, because the attention of many people naturally adds a sense of importance to them.

Understanding the opposite helps lock in the meaning. Something low-profile is deliberately kept quiet, out of the spotlight, and away from public attention. For example, a witness in a dangerous case might try to live a low-profile life — staying away from cameras, avoiding attention, not drawing notice to themselves. "High-profile" is the exact opposite: you are in the spotlight, whether you want to be or not.

Being high-profile is not always a choice. Sometimes a person or situation becomes high-profile simply because circumstances push them into the spotlight — for example, an ordinary person who witnesses a major historical event and suddenly finds the whole world interested in them. Other times, it is very deliberate — a company might launch a high-profile advertising campaign, intentionally designed to grab as much public attention as possible.

So the word can describe both accidental and intentional visibility.

• "The murder trial was a high-profile case that was broadcast live on television for weeks."

Here, the trial is being watched by a massive audience — it is extremely visible and talked about.

  • "She left her high-profile career in politics to live quietly in the countryside."

Her political career kept her constantly in the public eye. She chose to escape that spotlight.

  • "The company made a high-profile announcement about its new product at a packed press conference."

The announcement was made in a big, public, attention-grabbing way — not quietly or behind closed doors.

  • "He is one of the most high-profile figures in the fashion industry."

He is among the most recognized, talked-about, and visible people in that world.

If you had to remember just one thing: high-profile = attracting a great deal of public attention and visibility.

Everything else — the types of people, events, and situations it describes, the nuance of whether it's deliberate, the contrast with "low-profile" — all flows naturally from that single, clear core idea.
7629:
High-ranking means holding a position near or at the top of a structured group, organization, or system.

When people belong to an organization — an army, a government, a company, a police force — they are not all equal. Some people are at the bottom (they have little authority), some are in the middle, and some are at the very top (they have great authority). This arrangement of levels, from low to high, is called a hierarchy or a ranking system — think of it like a ladder, where each step is a different level of power and importance.

When we say someone is high-ranking, we mean they are near or at the top of that ladder. They hold a position of significant power, authority, and status within their organization or system.

The word is made of two parts:

  • High — near the top, of great importance
  • Ranking — referring to one's position or level within a hierarchy

Together, they form a single adjective that describes where someone stands within a formal structure — and the answer is: near the top.

When you call someone high-ranking, you are communicating several things at once:

Authority. A high-ranking person has power over the people below them. Their decisions carry weight. Others are expected to listen to them and follow their direction.

Prestige and respect. Within their organization, a high-ranking person is looked up to. Their title alone commands a level of respect from peers and subordinates.

Responsibility. High-ranking individuals are typically trusted with important decisions, sensitive information, and critical missions. The stakes involved in their work are usually much greater than those of people at lower levels.

A formal position. This is important — "high-ranking" refers strictly to an official position within a structured system. It does not mean someone is simply famous, popular, wealthy, or admired in a general social sense. A celebrity might be famous, but they are not "high-ranking" unless they also hold a formal position of authority within some organization.

The adjective "high-ranking" appears most naturally in formal or official contexts. Here are the most common ones:

Military. In an army, people have ranks — private, corporal, sergeant, lieutenant, captain, colonel, general. A general is high-ranking. A private is not. So you might read: "A high-ranking military officer attended the meeting."

Government. In a government, ministers, senators, ambassadors, and secretaries of state are high-ranking. A junior clerk in a government office is not. Example: "High-ranking officials gathered to discuss the crisis."

Business and corporations. A CEO, a vice-president, a chief financial officer — these are high-ranking within a company. An intern or a junior assistant is not. Example: "She is a high-ranking executive at the firm."

Law enforcement. A police chief or commissioner is high-ranking. A regular patrol officer is not. Example: "High-ranking officers were called in to oversee the investigation."

Religious institutions, universities, international organizations — the same principle applies anywhere there is a formal hierarchy.
The Relative Nature of the Word

This is a subtle but important point: "high-ranking" is relative, not absolute.

A captain in the army is high-ranking compared to a private or a corporal, but low-ranking compared to a general. The word tells you someone is towards the top of their particular group or system — not necessarily the most powerful person in the entire world.

Context always matters. When someone is called "a high-ranking official," you should ask: high-ranking within what organization? The answer tells you exactly how much authority that person holds.

It is not about personality. A high-ranking person can be kind or cruel, brilliant or incompetent. The word says nothing about who they are as a person — only where they sit in a hierarchy.

It is not about physical height. "High" here is purely metaphorical, referring to status, not height.

It is not about social fame or popularity. A beloved local artist or a social media star is not "high-ranking" in the sense this word is used. The word belongs to the world of formal structures and official power.

It is not permanent. Someone can be high-ranking today and lose that rank tomorrow through demotion, retirement, or dismissal.

• A high-ranking diplomat flew in to negotiate the peace deal.
  • The scandal involved several high-ranking members of the government.
  • She worked her way up from an entry-level job to become a high-ranking executive.
  • High-ranking officers in the military are responsible for commanding thousands of soldiers.
  • The investigation revealed that the corruption had reached high-ranking officials.

If you had to define it in one sentence: High-ranking describes a person who holds a powerful, authoritative, and prestigious position near or at the top of a formal organization or hierarchy, giving them significant influence and responsibility over others below them.
7630:
A high-rise is a very tall building with many floors, built upward rather than outward, and equipped with elevators so people can move between floors without climbing endless stairs.

Think of it this way: if you stand in a city and look up at a towering building that seems to stretch toward the sky — with dozens of windows stacked one above another — that is a high-rise.
What Exactly Makes a Building a "High-Rise"?

There is no single, universally agreed number of floors that officially makes a building a high-rise. However, in most practical and technical contexts, a building is generally considered a high-rise when it is roughly 7 or more stories tall — which is approximately 75 feet (about 23 metres) or higher. Some definitions place the threshold slightly higher, at around 10 or more stories.

The most important idea is not a strict number, but rather a set of qualities:

The building is tall enough that walking up and down stairs to reach every floor would be exhausting or impractical. Because of this, high-rises always have elevators (also called lifts) as the main way of traveling between floors. This is actually one of the defining features of a high-rise — its height forces a dependence on vertical transportation systems like elevators, and also demands special engineering, structural design, and safety systems such as fire suppression equipment and multiple emergency stairwells.

High-rises are not all the same type of building. They serve different purposes:

Residential high-rises are apartment buildings where people live. Each floor contains individual homes (called apartments or flats), and many families or individuals live stacked on top of one another within the same building. These are extremely common in dense cities where land is expensive and scarce, so building upward is the practical solution.

Commercial high-rises are used for business — most commonly as office buildings. Companies rent out entire floors or parts of floors, and thousands of workers come to these buildings each day to work.

Mixed-use high-rises combine both purposes — for example, the lower floors might contain shops, restaurants, or offices, while the upper floors are residential apartments.

Some high-rises also serve as hotels.
How Is a High-Rise Different from a Skyscraper?

This is an important distinction that confuses many learners.

A skyscraper is essentially a very extreme version of a high-rise — an exceptionally tall building that dramatically dominates the city skyline. Think of the Burj Khalifa in Dubai or the Empire State Building in New York. While there is overlap in how people use these words casually, in more technical usage, "skyscraper" implies a building that is extraordinarily tall, often 40 or more floors, and architecturally iconic. A high-rise is the broader, more general term — all skyscrapers are high-rises, but not all high-rises are skyscrapers.

On the other end of the scale, a mid-rise is a moderately tall building — typically around 5 to 12 floors — and a low-rise is a short building of just 1 to 4 floors (like a house or a small apartment building).

So the scale goes: low-rise → mid-rise → high-rise → skyscraper, with each step representing a taller, more complex building.

High-rises exist primarily because of limited land space in cities. Land in city centers is extremely expensive and scarce. Instead of building many small buildings spread across a wide area, it is more efficient to build one tall building on a small plot of land that can house hundreds or even thousands of people or workers. This is why you see clusters of high-rises in the centers of major cities like New York, Tokyo, Shanghai, Dubai, and Hong Kong.
How the Word Is Used in Sentences

Seeing a word in context is one of the best ways to understand it fully. Here are some natural examples:

  • "She moved into a high-rise on the 34th floor and loved the view of the city."
  • "The city council approved the construction of a new high-rise in the downtown area."
  • "He works in a glass high-rise near the financial district."
  • "The high-rise had 48 floors, three elevators, and a rooftop garden."

Notice that the word "high-rise" in all these examples refers to the building itself as a thing — that is the noun form.

If you had to remember just one thing: a high-rise is a tall building — typically 7 or more stories — that uses elevators, stands in an urban area, and is designed for people to live in, work in, or both.
7631:
High-strung describes a person who is very nervous, tense, and easily stressed or upset. A high-strung person has emotional and mental sensitivity that is turned up very high — they react intensely to things that other people might brush off or barely notice.

Think of it this way: imagine a dial that controls how strongly someone reacts to the world around them. Most people's dial is somewhere in the middle. A high-strung person's dial is cranked all the way up.
What It Looks Like in Real Life

A high-strung person typically shows some or many of these traits:

  • They worry a lot, often about things before they even happen.
  • They get anxious or agitated quickly — a small problem can feel like a big crisis to them.
  • They are easily irritated and can snap or get frustrated faster than most people.
  • They struggle to relax or stay calm, even when there is no real danger or emergency.
  • They may be restless — always moving, fidgeting, or unable to sit still mentally.
  • They tend to be highly sensitive to criticism, noise, change, or anything unexpected.
  • They often feel like they are always on edge, as if something bad could happen at any moment.

A classic example: You and a friend are waiting to hear if you passed an exam. You feel a little nervous but mostly calm. Your high-strung friend, however, cannot stop pacing, checks their phone every two minutes, overthinks every possible outcome, and can barely eat. That intensity — that inability to settle down — is what "high-strung" captures.
It Describes a Personality Trait, Not Just a Moment

This is an important distinction. Being high-strung is not about having one bad, stressful day. It is a consistent pattern — a part of someone's character and temperament. It describes the way someone generally is, not just how they feel on a particular occasion.

You would not call someone high-strung just because they were nervous before a job interview. But if that person is nervous, tense, and reactive in nearly every situation — that is high-strung.
It Can Apply to Animals Too

"High-strung" is also commonly used to describe animals, especially horses and dogs. A high-strung horse is one that is very skittish, easily startled, and hard to calm down. A high-strung dog might bark at everything, be unable to settle, and get overly excited or fearful very easily.
The Tone: Is It an Insult?

"High-strung" sits in a slightly negative to neutral zone. It is not a cruel insult, but it is not a compliment either. It is more of an observation about someone's nature.

People sometimes use it with sympathy ("She's just naturally high-strung — it's hard for her") and other times with mild frustration ("He's so high-strung; he overreacts to everything"). The tone depends entirely on who is saying it and how.

It is worth noting that a high-strung person often cannot simply choose to stop being that way. It is typically a deep part of who they are, sometimes linked to anxiety or a highly sensitive nervous system. So using the word to mock someone would be unkind.
How It Compares to Similar Words

Understanding "high-strung" becomes sharper when you compare it to related words:

  • Nervous — Nervous can be temporary ("I'm nervous about the speech"). High-strung is more permanent and built into personality.
  • Anxious — Very close in meaning. High-strung includes anxiety but also adds irritability, restlessness, and general emotional intensity.
  • Tense — Tense usually refers to a temporary physical or mental state. High-strung is a broader, more lasting quality.
  • Uptight — Very similar and nearly interchangeable in casual speech. "Uptight" leans a little more toward being rigid and unable to loosen up socially.
  • Wound up — Another near-synonym, often used in phrases like "too wound up to sleep."
  • Laid-back — The direct opposite of high-strung. A laid-back person is relaxed, easygoing, and hard to rattle.
  • Easygoing — Also an opposite. Where a high-strung person sees problems everywhere, an easygoing person takes things as they come.

Here are several sentences showing the word used naturally in context:

  • "My boss is incredibly high-strung — she panics over the smallest mistake."
  • "He's always been high-strung, even as a child. Loud noises would send him into tears."
  • "That high-strung energy makes her great in a fast-paced job, but exhausting to be around sometimes."
  • "The rescue dog was too high-strung for a family with young children."
  • "Try not to bring up the delays around her — she's high-strung enough as it is."

If you had to boil the entire word down to one sentence:

High-strung means someone is extremely nervous, tense, and emotionally reactive by nature — they are wound tightly inside and get stressed, anxious, or agitated much more easily and intensely than most people.

Hold that image — a person whose inner tension is always running high, who cannot easily switch off or calm down — and you will never forget what high-strung means.
7632:
When something is described as highbrow, it means it is intellectual, serious, and culturally sophisticated — the kind of thing associated with deep thinking, high education, and refined taste. It describes ideas, art, entertainment, or people that operate at a level that requires significant knowledge, intelligence, or cultural background to fully appreciate.

Think of it this way: highbrow things don't make life easy for you. They challenge you, demand your full attention, and expect you to bring some knowledge or education to the table.
What Kinds of Things Are Called "Highbrow"?

The word is used very broadly across culture and the arts:

  • Literature: A dense philosophical novel by Dostoevsky is highbrow. A gossip magazine is not.
  • Music: A classical symphony performed at a concert hall is highbrow. A catchy pop song on the radio is not.
  • Film: A slow, subtitled foreign film exploring the meaning of human existence is highbrow. A loud action blockbuster is not.
  • Conversation: Discussing the ethics of artificial intelligence or debating political philosophy is highbrow. Chatting about last night's football game is not.
  • Humour: A joke that depends on knowing Latin or referencing ancient Greek myths is highbrow humour.

The common thread in all these examples is intellectual seriousness and sophistication.

When you call a person highbrow, you mean they are deeply intellectual and tend to prefer serious, complex, or elite cultural experiences over popular ones. A highbrow person might spend their weekends reading academic essays, attending the opera, and discussing philosophy — and might have little interest in (or may even quietly look down on) simple, mass-market entertainment.

This is an important point: when used to describe people, "highbrow" often carries a slight edge of criticism. It can suggest that the person is a little snobby or elitist — that they consider themselves intellectually superior and look down on ordinary people's tastes.

So the word can be used in two slightly different ways:

  1. Neutral or admiring: "She has very highbrow taste in literature." (She reads serious, intellectual books — stated as a simple fact or even a compliment.)
  2. Mildly critical: "He's so highbrow — he refused to watch anything that isn't a foreign art film." (He's being a snob about it.)

The context and tone of the speaker's voice (or writing) usually make it clear which meaning is intended.

To truly understand "highbrow," it helps to know its opposite: lowbrow.

  • Lowbrow describes things (or people) that are simple, unsophisticated, and aimed at popular mass audiences — slapstick comedy, reality TV, fast food culture, trashy novels. There is no intellectual demand placed on you. You just consume and enjoy.
  • Highbrow is at the other end of the scale — demanding, intellectual, and often associated with elite or academic culture.
  • Right in the middle sits middlebrow — things that are reasonably intelligent and culturally respectable, but still accessible and enjoyable to a wide audience. A well-made historical drama on television, for example, might be described as middlebrow.

These three words together paint a full picture of the cultural spectrum.

Not necessarily, and this is a subtle but important point. Calling something highbrow is a description of its intellectual level and cultural style — it is not automatically a judgment of quality. Something can be highbrow and brilliant, but something can also be highbrow and boring, pretentious, or unnecessarily difficult. Equally, something lowbrow can be genuinely joyful, creative, and deeply entertaining.

The word tells you what kind of thing it is, not whether it is good or bad.

• "The documentary was a little too highbrow for me — I couldn't follow all the philosophical references."
  • "She moved in highbrow intellectual circles, attending lectures and literary salons."
  • "The magazine tried to strike a balance between highbrow analysis and stories that everyday readers could enjoy."
  • "His humour was so highbrow that half the audience didn't get the jokes."
  • "The play was considered highbrow entertainment — the kind of thing critics loved but general audiences avoided."
Highbrow means intellectually sophisticated, serious, and associated with elite culture and education — and when used about people, it can suggest they are a bit of a snob about it.
7633:
When you call something highfalutin, you are saying it is trying too hard to seem grand, impressive, or important — but in a way that feels fake, overdone, or unnecessary. It is the word you reach for when something (or someone) is puffed up with a sense of its own importance.

Think of it this way: imagine a person who uses ten complicated words when one simple word would do just fine, who speaks in a grand, theatrical voice even in casual conversation, and who acts as though everything they say deserves to be carved in stone. That person — or their speech, or their attitude — is highfalutin.
The Three Main Things It Describes

Highfalutin is most commonly used to describe three things: language, behavior, and ideas.

1. Highfalutin language is language that is unnecessarily fancy, flowery, or complicated. It uses big, impressive-sounding words or overly elaborate sentences where plain, simple language would communicate the same thing far more clearly. The speaker or writer seems to be more interested in sounding sophisticated than in actually saying something useful. A politician who uses long, ornate sentences stuffed with jargon to say something that could be said in ten plain words is using highfalutin language.

2. Highfalutin behavior refers to acting in a way that is snobbish, self-important, or superior — as if the person is above ordinary people or ordinary things. It is the attitude of someone who puts on airs, meaning they perform a level of refinement or importance that is exaggerated or unearned. A neighbor who refuses to attend community events because they consider them "beneath" them has a highfalutin attitude.

3. Highfalutin ideas or plans are ones that are grandiose — far more ambitious or lofty in their presentation than they deserve to be, or wildly impractical in their scope. When someone frames a very ordinary goal in enormous, sweeping, dramatic terms — as though they are about to change the fate of civilization — their plans sound highfalutin.

This is important: highfalutin is not a neutral word. When you use it, you are almost always mocking or criticizing what you are describing, even if gently. You are rolling your eyes. You are saying, in effect: "Come on. Drop the act. This is not as impressive as it's being made to sound."

The word itself has a folksy, down-to-earth flavor. There is something almost deliberately unpretentious about it — which is exactly why it works so well to puncture pretension. A plain-spoken farmer calling a city lawyer's speech "highfalutin" captures the attitude perfectly.

This means the word often carries a slight sense of humor — a gentle, knowing smirk. It is not usually an angry insult. It is more of a wry, grounded observation that something is overdressed and overblown.
The Spectrum: Mild vs. Strong Use

The word can be used across a range of intensities.

On the milder end, you might use it affectionately or playfully — "you don't need all those highfalutin words with me" said to a friend who just showed off their vocabulary. Here, it's teasing.

On the stronger end, it can be a real criticism — "the company's mission statement is full of highfalutin language that means nothing" — suggesting that the fancy words are actually hiding an emptiness of substance.

To sharpen the definition, it helps to draw some boundaries.

Highfalutin does not simply mean complicated. A physics textbook is complicated, but it is not highfalutin — the complexity serves a real purpose. Highfalutin means the complexity (or grandeur, or fanciness) is unwarranted — it exists for show.

Highfalutin does not simply mean formal. A formal speech at a graduation is not automatically highfalutin. But if that speech becomes so stuffed with grand, hollow phrases that it loses meaning entirely, it tips into being highfalutin.

The key element is always the gap between appearance and reality — something presenting itself as more elevated, important, or sophisticated than it truly is.

• "I just asked him what time the meeting starts, and he gave me this highfalutin speech about the nature of time management. Just answer the question!"
  • "The restaurant had a highfalutin menu — every dish had a three-paragraph description, but the food was nothing special."
  • "She has some highfalutin ideas about rebranding the entire company, but no actual plan for how to do it."
  • "He's a bit highfalutin for my taste — he corrects everyone's grammar at dinner parties."
  • "Stop using those highfalutin words. Just say what you mean."

To further anchor the meaning, here are words that share its territory: pompous, pretentious, grandiose, bombastic, snobbish, self-important, affected, ostentatious, inflated. Among these, pretentious and pompous are its closest cousins in everyday use. However, highfalutin is distinctly more informal, more colorful, and carries a more playful, folksy edge than any of those alternatives — it is the word a person with their feet firmly on the ground would use.

If you need to lock it into one sentence: Highfalutin describes something or someone that is excessively grand, fancy, or self-important in a way that feels fake, overdone, or unearned — and the word is almost always used to mock or gently deflate that pretension.
7634:
To highlight something means to draw special attention to it — to pull it out from everything around it and say, "Look at this. This matters."

Think of it this way: imagine a page full of text. Every sentence is there, but they all look the same. Now you take a bright yellow marker and color over one important sentence. Instantly, that sentence stands apart. Your eye goes straight to it. You have highlighted it.

That physical image — making one thing visibly stand out from a crowd of things — is the heart of what this verb means, in every context where it is used.
The Three Main Ways It Is Used

1. The Physical Act (with a pen or marker)

You use a highlighter pen to mark text on paper in a bright color, so that specific part is easy to find again.

She highlighted every definition in her textbook before the exam.

He highlighted the three sentences his professor had said were most important.

Here, the act is literal and visual. The highlighted text glows against the rest of the page.

2. The Digital Act (on a screen)

On a computer, phone, or tablet, when you click and drag your cursor over text, it gets selected — it appears with a colored background. This is also called highlighting.

Highlight the paragraph and then press Delete.

He highlighted the URL in the browser bar and copied it.

This is the same idea — you are selecting something, making it visually distinct, separating it from the rest.

3. The Figurative Act (the most important use)

This is where "highlight" is used most widely in English — not with a pen or screen, but through speech, writing, or action. When you highlight something in this sense, you bring it to people's attention. You emphasize it. You make sure it is noticed and considered, rather than overlooked.

The doctor highlighted the risks of the surgery before the patient signed the form.

The report highlighted three major problems in the company's finances.

In her speech, the president highlighted the need for better schools.

The documentary highlights how climate change is affecting small island nations.

In all these examples, no marker is used. Instead, the speaker or writer is choosing to bring certain information forward — to the front of the listener's or reader's mind — while other information stays in the background.
What Makes "Highlight" Different From Similar Words

Several words are close in meaning — mention, state, emphasize, stress, point out, underscore, spotlight. But "highlight" carries a specific feeling:

  • Mention is casual. You just say something in passing. It carries no special weight.
  • State is neutral. You are simply declaring a fact.
  • Highlight implies selection and importance. When you highlight something, you have made a deliberate choice: out of many things you could say, you are making this stand out. There is a built-in message: this is worth your attention.

Highlighting is always intentional. Nobody accidentally highlights something. The choice of what to highlight — and what not to — reveals what you consider important.

When you highlight something, you are always making a judgment: this is significant. This is true whether you are being positive, critical, or neutral.

Positive — highlighting an achievement or strength:

The manager highlighted her team's exceptional performance during the meeting.

Critical — highlighting a flaw, problem, or concern:

The investigation highlighted serious failures in the safety system.

Neutral — highlighting a fact or difference:

The study highlights the differences in how men and women experience stress.

The word itself has no emotional color. It does not tell you whether the highlighted thing is good or bad. That depends on what is being highlighted. The word simply tells you: attention is being deliberately placed here.

It does not mean to explain fully. You can highlight a problem without going into every detail. Highlighting is about pointing attention, not providing a complete analysis.

It does not mean to exaggerate. Highlighting brings something forward — it doesn't distort it or make it bigger than it is. (If someone exaggerates, we would say they overstated or inflated, not highlighted.)

It does not mean to discover. You highlight something that already exists. You are not finding it for the first time — you are making sure others notice it.

You will notice that "highlight" appears frequently with these kinds of objects:

  • highlight a problem / an issue / a concern
  • highlight the importance of something
  • highlight the need for something
  • highlight a difference / a contrast
  • highlight an achievement / a success
  • highlight a risk / a danger
  • highlight key findings / key points
  • highlight the fact that...

These patterns show you that what gets highlighted is almost always something the speaker considers significant — something they do not want lost in the crowd.
One More Nuance: What Is Left in the Shadow

Here is something subtle but important: when you highlight one thing, you are also not highlighting everything else. This means highlighting involves a kind of judgment about priority.

If a journalist writes a report about a company and highlights only its profits while not highlighting its environmental damage, that is a choice that shapes what readers notice and care about. This is why, in debates and arguments, people sometimes challenge what others choose to highlight — because choosing what stands out is a form of influence.

To highlight (verb) means: to deliberately draw attention to something, making it stand out as important or worthy of notice — whether you are doing this with a marker on paper, by selecting text on a screen, or by choosing to emphasize certain information in speech or writing.

The key ideas are: selection, intention, and attention. You pick something. You bring it forward. You make it impossible to ignore.
7635:
In everyday English, hijab refers to the headscarf worn by many Muslim women — a piece of fabric that covers the hair, ears, and neck, while leaving the face fully visible. If you pass a Muslim woman on the street wearing a scarf wrapped around her head, that covering is what most people in the English-speaking world call a hijab.

But that one-sentence answer only scratches the surface. The word carries a much richer meaning.
The Deeper Meaning: More Than a Scarf

In its fuller, original sense — rooted in Islamic thought — "hijab" does not just mean a piece of cloth. It refers to the principle of modesty and moral conduct itself. This includes how a person dresses, how they behave, how they speak, and how they carry themselves in public. In this broader sense, hijab is a way of being, not just a garment.

Think of it this way: the headscarf is the visible expression of hijab, but hijab as a concept is the internal value of modesty that the scarf represents outwardly.

So when someone says, "She wears hijab," they usually mean she wears the headscarf. But when a scholar or devout Muslim speaks of "observing hijab," they mean living by a whole standard of modesty — in dress, in speech, and in behavior.
What the Physical Garment Looks Like

As a physical item, a hijab:

  • Covers the hair, ears, and neck completely
  • Leaves the face entirely open and visible
  • Is typically a square or rectangular piece of fabric, wrapped or pinned around the head in various styles
  • Can be made of cotton, polyester, silk, chiffon, or many other fabrics
  • Comes in every color, pattern, and style imaginable — from plain black to bright florals

The way a hijab is styled varies enormously. Some women wrap it tightly and simply. Others pin it loosely and drape it elegantly. Some tuck it into their collar, others let it rest on their shoulders. There is no single "correct" look.
How It Differs from Other Islamic Coverings

Many people confuse hijab with other types of Islamic head or face coverings. They are different garments, and the distinctions matter:

Niqab — covers the entire face except for the eyes. The eyes remain visible through a narrow slit or opening. A woman wearing a niqab also usually wears a hijab underneath or alongside it.

Burqa — covers the entire body, head, and face. Even the eyes are covered, typically with a fine mesh screen to see through. The burqa is most closely associated with certain regions of Afghanistan and Pakistan.

Chador — a full-length cloak, usually black, that drapes over the head and wraps around the entire body, held shut from the inside. It typically does not cover the face. It is common in Iran.

Jilbab — a long, loose outer garment that covers the body from shoulders to ankles, often worn alongside a hijab. It is not a head covering itself, but a full-body outer robe.

The hijab specifically is just the head covering that leaves the face exposed. It is the most widely worn of all these coverings and the most commonly encountered in Western countries.

Hijab is worn by Muslim women. Most commonly, women begin wearing it around the time of puberty, though this varies by family, culture, and personal conviction. In some families, girls start wearing it earlier; in others, women choose to begin in adulthood.

The reasons a woman wears hijab are deeply personal and vary widely:

Religious obligation — Many Muslim women wear hijab because they believe their faith requires it. Verses in the Quran (Islam's holy book) and sayings attributed to the Prophet Muhammad call for modesty in dress, and many scholars have interpreted these as requiring women to cover their hair when in public or in the presence of men outside their immediate family.

Personal faith and identity — Even among those who may not see it as strictly obligatory, many women wear it as a powerful expression of their identity as Muslim women — a visible, daily declaration of their beliefs.

Cultural and community practice — In some Muslim families and communities, wearing hijab is simply the cultural norm passed down through generations, much like any other dress tradition.

Personal empowerment — Some women describe wearing hijab as empowering — a rejection of being judged by physical appearance, a statement that they are defined by their mind and character, not their looks.

Spirituality and discipline — For many, the daily act of putting on hijab is a spiritual practice — a mindful reminder of their values and their relationship with God.
Is It Compulsory? The Ongoing Debate

This is one of the most debated questions in contemporary Islam, and there is no single answer that all Muslims agree on.

Those who consider it obligatory point to specific Quranic verses (particularly Chapter 24, verse 31, and Chapter 33, verse 59) and to Islamic scholarly tradition, which has historically interpreted these passages as requiring Muslim women to cover their hair in public. For these Muslims — and they represent a large part of the Muslim world — hijab is a religious duty, not merely a suggestion.

Those who consider it a personal choice argue that the Quranic verses speak more broadly about modesty and that the specific requirement to cover the hair is a matter of cultural interpretation rather than divine command. They may see modesty in dress as important without believing the headscarf specifically is required.

Political and governmental dimensions add another layer. Some countries — like Iran and Saudi Arabia — have at various times legally required women to wear hijab in public. Other countries — like France — have at times legally restricted or banned it in certain public spaces. These laws affect women regardless of their personal beliefs, meaning some wear hijab by law, and some are prevented from wearing it by law. Both situations have generated major controversy and human rights debates worldwide.

The key point: a woman wearing hijab may be doing so by personal conviction, family tradition, religious belief, cultural identity, legal requirement, or any combination of these. A woman not wearing hijab may also be Muslim and devout. Hijab does not define a woman's level of faith or religiousness.

While hijab is most commonly discussed in relation to women's dress, the concept of hijab in its broad sense applies to men too. Islamic teaching calls on men to observe modesty — in how they dress (typically covering from navel to knee at minimum), in how they lower their gaze in the presence of women, and in how they conduct themselves. The physical garment called "hijab" is female-specific, but the underlying value of modesty it represents is universal in Islamic ethics.

In modern, everyday English, when someone says "hijab," they almost always mean the headscarf — the physical garment. The broader philosophical meaning is mostly used in religious, academic, or deeply faith-based contexts.

You might hear it used like this:

  • "She started wearing hijab last year."
  • "The school had a debate about allowing students to wear hijab."
  • "She chose not to wear hijab, but she considers herself a practicing Muslim."

In all these cases, "hijab" = the headscarf.

Hijab is a headscarf worn by many Muslim women, covering the hair, ears, and neck while leaving the face visible. At its deepest, it is a concept of modesty — a set of values about dress, behavior, and moral conduct rooted in Islamic faith. It is not a face veil (that is the niqab), not a full-body covering (that is the burqa), and not a long outer robe (that is the jilbab). It is worn for reasons ranging from religious duty to personal identity to cultural practice. Whether it is obligatory or optional is a question Muslims actively debate. And it is, for hundreds of millions of women around the world, a deeply meaningful and personal part of how they live their faith.
7636:
To hijack something means to forcefully take control of something that is already in motion or already underway, without permission, and redirect it toward your own purpose — against the will of whoever was rightfully in charge of it.

Three things are always happening at once when something is hijacked:

  1. Something was already moving or in progress, headed toward a specific goal.
  2. Someone seized control of it by force, threat, or aggressive pressure — without any right to do so.
  3. The original plan was interrupted and pulled in a completely different direction.

That combination — force + interception + redirection — is the soul of this word.

The clearest, most direct use of "hijack" is about vehicles. Picture this:

A plane takes off from New York, bound for London. Midway through the flight, a person threatens the pilots and says, "Don't fly to London. Fly to Cuba instead." The pilots comply because they have no choice. That person has just hijacked the plane.

The same thing can happen to a bus, a ship, or a truck. The person who does it is called a hijacker, and the act itself is called a hijacking. These are serious violent crimes. The hijacker's goal might be to make a political demand, rob the vehicle and its passengers, or escape somewhere without going through normal channels.

The key detail is that the vehicle was already in use, already on its way somewhere — the hijacker didn't steal an empty parked vehicle. They intercepted it mid-journey and took the wheel.
The Extended Meaning: Far Beyond Vehicles

This is where "hijack" becomes a truly powerful word to know, because modern English uses it constantly in non-vehicle situations. Wherever something is already underway and someone aggressively takes it over and steers it toward their own agenda, the word fits perfectly.

A conversation:
"She tried to talk about her problems, but her roommate hijacked the conversation and spent an hour talking about himself."
The conversation was already in motion. He took it over and redirected it — without her consent.

A meeting:
"The CEO had a clear agenda, but angry shareholders hijacked the meeting with demands he wasn't prepared for."
The meeting had a planned direction. It was forcefully pulled somewhere else.

A political or social movement:
"The peaceful protest was hijacked by a group of extremists who had a completely different agenda."
The movement stood for one thing; others took it over and redirected its energy for their own goals.

An idea or a plan:
"She came up with the entire concept, but her colleague hijacked it and presented it to the boss as his own."

An online hashtag:
"A company launched a feel-good hashtag campaign, but users hijacked it to publicly criticize the company's labor practices."
The company created the hashtag for one purpose; thousands of people seized it and steered it in the opposite direction.

In every single case, you'll find the same three elements: something already in motion → someone forcefully seizes control → it gets redirected away from its original purpose.

In computing and cybersecurity, "hijack" is used frequently and precisely:

Browser hijacking is when malicious software secretly takes control of your web browser — changing your homepage, redirecting your searches to different websites, or opening pages you never asked for. You didn't consent; something took over your browser and started steering it.

Session hijacking is when a hacker intercepts an active, ongoing connection between you and a website (say, your online bank account) and takes it over — pretending to be you.

DNS hijacking is when internet traffic you intended to send to one website gets secretly rerouted to a different one.

The pattern is the same: something already active and in use gets forcefully taken over and redirected without authorization.
The Weight and Feeling of the Word

"Hijack" is a strong, dramatic word. It is never neutral. When you use it, it always carries these feelings:

Aggression — The takeover wasn't gentle or polite. It was forced. Even when there's no physical weapon involved (as in a hijacked conversation), the word signals dominance, pressure, or manipulation.

Illegitimacy — The person taking control has no right to be in control. They are an intruder.

Violation — The rightful owner or operator loses control against their will. Something is being stolen from them — not a physical object, but direction, purpose, and authority.

This is why saying "he hijacked the conversation" is much stronger than saying "he changed the subject." You're signaling that it wasn't a polite shift — it was a hostile, unwanted takeover.

Hijack vs. Steal:
You steal a parked car from a parking lot. You hijack a moving bus. Stealing is about taking possession of something idle. Hijacking is about intercepting something that is actively in use and in motion.

Hijack vs. Take over:
"Take over" is neutral and can be perfectly legal — a company can take over another company through a proper business deal. "Hijack" always implies it is unauthorized, forced, and wrong.

Hijack vs. Commandeer:
To commandeer is to officially seize something by authority — like a military officer commandeering a civilian vehicle in wartime. It sounds formal and sanctioned. To hijack is always unauthorized and criminal or at least inappropriate.

Hijack vs. Derail:
To derail something means to disrupt and ruin it — knock it off course so it goes nowhere. To hijack something means to disrupt it AND then steer it toward your own destination. Derailing destroys the journey. Hijacking steals the journey.

To hijack something means:

→ To forcefully take control of something already in motion or in progress
→ Without permission, against the will of whoever is rightfully in charge
→ And redirect it for your own purpose

It works in the literal sense (seizing planes, buses, ships mid-journey), in everyday social situations (conversations, meetings, movements, ideas), and in the digital world (browsers, internet sessions, online trends).

Whenever you see or hear "hijack," picture someone grabbing the steering wheel of a moving vehicle from the driver's hands — that image captures the force, the wrongness, and the redirection that the word always carries, no matter what context it appears in.
7637: Hike has two completely separate, unrelated meanings depending on the context. A third, specialized meaning exists in American football. Here is each one explained fully.
Meaning 1 — A Long Walk in Nature

A hike is a long walk taken outdoors, on natural terrain such as mountains, forests, hills, valleys, or countryside trails.

What makes a hike different from a regular walk?

A walk is casual and can happen anywhere — on a street, in a mall, around a park. A hike is different in three key ways:

  • It happens in a natural, outdoor setting (not in a city or on paved roads).
  • It is physically more demanding — it involves climbing, uneven ground, or long distances.
  • It usually takes a significant amount of time, often hours.

People go on hikes for enjoyment, fitness, adventure, or to experience nature.

Examples in sentences:

  • "We went on a hike through the mountains."
  • "The hike to the waterfall was beautiful but tiring."
  • "It's a three-hour hike to the top."

Common descriptive phrases:

  • A short hike vs. a long hike — refers to distance or time.
  • A tough hike vs. an easy hike — refers to physical difficulty.
  • A scenic hike — a hike with beautiful views along the way.
  • A day hike — a hike completed within a single day, without camping overnight.
Meaning 2 — A Significant Increase (in price, rate, or cost)

This meaning is very commonly found in news, economics, and everyday conversations about money.

A hike here means a noticeable, sharp increase — usually in something financial, such as prices, taxes, wages, interest rates, or fees.

Key nuance: The word "hike" is not used for tiny, barely-noticeable increases. It signals a change that is large enough to be felt and noticed. It often carries a slightly negative tone — the people affected by the increase usually did not welcome it.

Examples in sentences:

  • "There has been a hike in fuel prices." → Fuel became more expensive.
  • "The government announced a tax hike." → Taxes went up significantly.
  • "The workers demanded a pay hike." → They wanted a notable raise in salary.
  • "The bank approved an interest rate hike." → Borrowing money became more expensive.

Very common fixed combinations (you will hear these constantly):

  • Price hike — an increase in the cost of goods or services.
  • Tax hike — an increase in taxes people must pay.
  • Rate hike — an increase in interest rates (used heavily in banking and economics).
  • Pay hike / Wage hike — an increase in salary or hourly wages.
  • Fare hike — an increase in the price of public transport (bus, train, etc.).
  • Rent hike — an increase in how much someone pays to live somewhere.

This meaning is narrow and only applies to the sport of American football.

A hike is the act of the center (a specific player on the team) snapping — that is, passing the ball backward between their legs — to the quarterback to officially start a play. The word is also used as a command: "Hike!" means "start the play now."

You only need this meaning if you watch or discuss American football.
How to Always Know Which Meaning Is Intended

Since the two main meanings are completely unrelated, the surrounding words in a sentence will always make it obvious:

  • If the sentence is about nature, walking, trails, or outdoors → it is Meaning 1.
  • If the sentence is about money, prices, taxes, rates, or wages → it is Meaning 2.
  • If the sentence is about American football → it is Meaning 3.

There is never any real ambiguity in practice.

"Hike" as a noun always contains the idea of something going up — either your body moving up and through nature on a long walk, or a number rising sharply. That mental image of "upward movement" is a useful thread connecting both major meanings.
7638:
Meaning 1: To walk a long distance, especially in nature

This is the most common meaning. When you hike, you walk a long distance — usually through mountains, forests, hills, or countryside. It is not just any walk. It carries the sense of physical effort, distance, and being in an outdoor, natural setting.

Examples:

  • "We hiked through the forest for six hours."
  • "She hiked along the river trail every weekend."
  • "They hiked ten miles before setting up camp."

What separates hiking from ordinary walking:

  • The terrain is usually uneven, steep, or rough — not a flat city pavement.
  • It takes much longer — usually hours.
  • It involves noticeable physical effort.
  • It happens in nature, and often for recreation or adventure.

You can also say "go hiking" (this is equally common):

  • "Let's go hiking this Sunday."
  • "Have you ever gone hiking in the mountains?"

Both mean the same thing — the only difference is phrasing.
Meaning 2: To raise or increase something sharply

In this sense, "hike" means to increase a price, rate, tax, salary, or fee — usually by a large amount, and often suddenly or unexpectedly. This meaning is very common in news, business, and economic conversation.

Examples:

  • "The government hiked fuel prices by 20%."
  • "The central bank hiked interest rates to slow down inflation."
  • "The landlord hiked the rent without warning."
  • "Airlines hiked ticket prices during the holiday season."

Important nuance — tone: Saying someone "hiked" a price sounds more alarming and dramatic than saying they "raised" or "increased" it. The word "hike" quietly suggests that the increase is steep, unwelcome, or abrupt. Journalists and writers use it precisely for this reason — it adds a sense of urgency or criticism.

So: "The company raised its prices" feels neutral. "The company hiked its prices" sounds sharper — almost like a complaint.

What can be "hiked" in this sense: Almost always something measurable — prices, fares, fees, taxes, interest rates, wages, costs. You would not use "hike" for vague or abstract things.
Meaning 3: To pull something upward sharply

This meaning is more physical and everyday. When you "hike" something, you grab it and pull it up firmly and quickly — usually a piece of clothing that has slipped down or needs to be raised.

This meaning almost always appears as the phrasal verb "hike up", not "hike" alone.

Examples:

  • "She hiked up her skirt to cross the muddy stream."
  • "He hiked up his trousers before kneeling on the floor."
  • "The child hiked up his socks."

The image is of a quick, firm yank upward — not a slow, gentle lift.
The Phrasal Verb "Hike Up" — Used for Both Meaning 2 and Meaning 3

You will notice that "hike up" works for both:

  • "They hiked up the prices." → raised the prices (Meaning 2)
  • "She hiked up her sleeve." → pulled her sleeve up (Meaning 3)

The context makes it clear which meaning is intended. If it is followed by clothing, it means to pull up. If it is followed by a price, cost, rate, or fee, it means to raise.
Register and Tone — When Is Each Meaning Used?

Nature/walking sense: Used in both casual and formal speech. Universally common.

Price/rate sense: Very common in journalism, economics, and business conversation. Carries a slightly negative, dramatic tone — implying the increase was large or unwelcome. Not used for small, expected increases.

Pull-up sense: Casual and informal, mostly in everyday spoken or written language.
The Three Meanings at a Glance

1. Walk long distances in nature → "They hiked the mountain trail."
  2. Raise prices/rates sharply → "The bank hiked interest rates."
  3. Pull clothing upward → "He hiked up his trousers."
7639:
Hilarious means extremely funny — so funny that it makes you laugh hard, loudly, or even uncontrollably. It is not just "a little funny" or "mildly amusing." It is the kind of funny that makes you burst out laughing, maybe even struggle to breathe or hold your stomach.

Think of it as sitting on a scale of funniness:

Amusing → Funny → Very funny → Hilarious → Side-splitting

"Amusing" is when something makes you smile gently. "Funny" is when you chuckle. "Hilarious" is when you laugh so hard you can't stop — it sits near the top of that scale.

Almost anything that makes people laugh intensely can be described as hilarious:

  • A joke — "He told a hilarious joke at the party."
  • A movie or TV show — "That comedy film was absolutely hilarious."
  • A situation — "It was a hilarious moment when the dog stole the wedding cake."
  • A person — "She is hilarious — everything she says makes me laugh."
  • A story or anecdote — "He shared a hilarious story about getting lost in Tokyo."
  • A video or post — "That meme is hilarious!"
  • Something unexpected or absurd — "The look on his face was hilarious."

When you call a person hilarious, you mean they are naturally and consistently very funny — they have a gift for making people laugh.
How intense is the laughter it describes?

The laughter "hilarious" points to is not polite or soft. It is loud, real, and often hard to control. You might:

  • laugh until your eyes water
  • slap your knee
  • double over
  • struggle to speak because you're laughing so much

If something is merely funny, people chuckle. If something is hilarious, people lose it.
How it is used in everyday speech

Hilarious is very common in casual, everyday English. People use it freely — sometimes even slightly exaggerated — to express that something was really, really funny.

Common patterns you will hear:

  • "That was hilarious!" (after something funny happens)
  • "I find him absolutely hilarious."
  • "We were laughing at the most hilarious thing."
  • "You have to watch this — it's hilarious."

Common words paired with it (collocations):

  • absolutely hilarious — the most common pairing; adds emphasis
  • utterly hilarious — same meaning, slightly more formal
  • genuinely hilarious — stresses that it is truly funny, not just a polite compliment
  • pretty hilarious — softer; means quite funny
  • find something hilarious — "I found the whole situation hilarious."

Sometimes "hilarious" is used sarcastically — meaning the opposite of what it literally says. The tone of voice (or context in writing) makes this clear.

For example, if someone plays an annoying prank on you and you say, "Oh, hilarious," with a flat or cold tone, you actually mean: "That was not funny at all."

This sarcastic use is common in real-life conversation and informal writing. Context always tells you which meaning is intended.
How it differs from similar words

WordWhat it meansIntensity of laughter
AmusingMildly entertaining; makes you smileA gentle smile
FunnyGeneral term for something that causes laughterA chuckle
ComicalFunny in a silly, clownish, or visual wayA laugh
HumorousHas a quality of humor; gentler, more thoughtfulA soft laugh or smile
HilariousExtremely funny; causes hard, uncontrollable laughterLoud, intense laughter
  • Amusing is gentle. A mildly entertaining story is amusing, not hilarious.
  • Funny is the everyday, middle-ground word. Most things that make you laugh are "funny."
  • Comical usually describes something visually silly — like a person falling in a clumsy way, or a ridiculous costume.
  • Humorous has a more intelligent, refined feel — a clever essay can be humorous even if it never makes you laugh loudly.
  • Hilarious is the strongest of these in terms of the intensity of laughter it describes.

• Hilariously (adverb) — describes how something is done in a funny way.
    "The cat hilariously knocked the glass off the table."
    "His speech was hilariously bad."
  • Hilarity (noun) — the state or quality of being very funny; the laughter and fun that results.
    "The room erupted in hilarity."
    "Much hilarity followed when the clown tripped."

Hilarious = extremely funny; causes intense, hard-to-control laughter.

It is stronger than "funny." It describes jokes, situations, people, videos, or stories that make people laugh loudly and fully. It is used freely in casual conversation, sometimes with slight exaggeration, and occasionally sarcastically to mean the opposite.
7640: Hilarity means a state of great, often loud and uncontrollable laughter and amusement — usually shared among a group of people. It is not just "being happy" or "finding something a little funny." It is the peak of amusement. Think of that moment at a dinner table where someone says something so funny that everyone bursts out laughing at the same time and can barely stop — that collective explosion of laughter is hilarity.

There are two slightly different ways this word is used, and both are correct:

1. Hilarity as a state people are in.
This is when a group of people are in a state of great laughter and amusement.

"The comedian's joke sent the whole room into hilarity."

Here, hilarity is the state the audience entered — they were all laughing loudly together.
